title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 35
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Turning the Ground
passages.text:
A. The plough is usually described as a labour-saving device, and for most of its history it was not. Breaking ground with a plough required a team of draught animals, the fodder to keep them, and often several people to manage the operation, which is a great deal of input for a task that a person with a hoe can accomplish on a small plot. What the plough offered was not less work per field but more field per household.

B. Soil type determined which design could be used and therefore what could be farmed. A light scratch plough suffices on thin dry soils and fails entirely on the heavy wet clays that hold the most nutrients; turning those requires a heavier implement, a cutting edge ahead of the share, and a board to invert the furrow. Regions differed in agricultural productivity for centuries according to whether their soil matched the available tool.

C. The heavy plough restructured the society that used it. It required more animals than a single household could keep, so teams were shared, and shared teams need agreement about sequence, timing and access — which favoured settlement patterns and field layouts organised for collective use. The technology did not simply serve an existing social arrangement; it selected for one.

D. Mechanisation broke the link between farm size and the labour available. A household could work only as much land as its own members and animals could manage, so farm size was bounded by biology; an engine removed that bound, and holdings consolidated wherever the machinery was affordable. The resulting depopulation of agricultural districts was not a side effect of mechanisation but the same event described from the other direction.

E. What machinery did to soil took much longer to notice. Heavier equipment compacts ground below the depth that cultivation reaches, reducing the capacity of roots to penetrate and of water to drain, and the damage accumulates invisibly over years. Practices that reduce it — controlled traffic, reduced tillage, lighter passes — spread slowly because the cost is deferred and the benefit is a loss that does not occur.

F. The current direction reverses a long trend towards uniformity. Equipment that varies its treatment across a single field according to measured soil conditions applies inputs where they are needed rather than evenly, which reduces both cost and runoff. It is the first substantial move away from treating a field as a single unit since the plough made treating it as one worthwhile.

passages.title: Where Rain Comes From
passages.text:
Rain requires more than water vapour and cooling, which is the fact that makes weather modification such a difficult business. Water does not readily condense on nothing: it needs a surface, and in the atmosphere that surface is provided by minute particles of dust, salt, soot and biological material. Without them, air can hold far more moisture than saturation would suggest and still produce nothing at all.

Given particles, a cloud forms and most clouds still do not rain. The droplets that condense are far too small to fall, and turning a cloud of suspended droplets into precipitation requires them to combine into drops heavy enough to overcome the updraught that holds them. The processes that achieve this — collision between droplets of differing size, and the growth of ice crystals at the expense of surrounding droplets — are inefficient, which is why a sky full of cloud is not a sky full of rain.

The ice process matters more than its share of visible cloud suggests. In a cloud containing both ice and supercooled liquid water, the ice grows while the droplets evaporate, because the conditions that keep water liquid below freezing also favour deposition onto ice. Much of the rain falling in temperate regions began as snow that melted on the way down, including rain in summer.

Attempts to induce rain rest on this mechanism and have been running for many decades. Introducing particles that promote ice formation into a suitable cloud should accelerate the process, and it demonstrably does so under controlled conditions. Whether it increases rainfall at the ground, over an area, in quantities worth the cost, is a different question and a considerably harder one.

The evaluation problem is the reason for the long dispute rather than any shortage of trials. Rainfall is highly variable in space and time, the counterfactual — what this cloud would have produced untreated — is unobservable, and the operations are typically conducted precisely when rain was already likely. Detecting a modest percentage change against that background requires very large samples over long periods, and the trials that meet those standards report smaller effects than the industry's claims.

The honest position is narrower than either side's summary of it. Under specific conditions, in particular cloud types, with careful targeting, modest increases have been measured and are real. General rain-making on demand, drought relief on a regional scale, and the claims made in procurement documents are not supported, and the persistence of the practice owes something to the fact that a treated season with rain is indistinguishable from an untreated one.

passages.title: The Cost of Being Looked After
passages.text:
Childcare has an economic structure that makes it expensive for reasons no policy can remove. The service is labour, delivered in person, with a ratio of adults to children below which it stops being safe, and this ratio is the binding cost. Productivity gains that reduce prices elsewhere are unavailable: one adult cannot look after twice as many infants using better equipment, and any improvement in efficiency is a reduction in the quality of the thing being bought.

That structure produces a persistent gap between what the service costs and what the households needing it can pay. Demand is concentrated in the years when earnings are lowest, since people have children early in their careers, and the fee for two children can exceed a second income entirely. The result is a decision that presents itself as a preference and is frequently an arithmetic conclusion.

The consequence falls unevenly and durably. The parent who leaves the labour market is usually the lower earner and usually the mother, and the earnings loss is not confined to the years away: it continues through slower progression, forgone seniority and reduced pension contributions for decades afterwards. A gap of a few years produces a lifetime difference substantially larger than the wages missed during it.

Public subsidy takes three forms and they behave differently. Payments to parents allow choice and are absorbed into higher prices where supply is constrained; payments to providers control price and quality but reduce flexibility; direct public provision guarantees availability and is expensive and slow to expand. Countries that achieved high participation combined a supply commitment with a price cap, which is the arrangement most difficult to legislate because its cost appears immediately and its return does not.

The return is real and arrives in a form no budget captures. Higher parental employment produces tax revenue and reduced benefit expenditure; the effects on children are measurable and concentrated among those from the least advantaged homes, for whom good provision produces gains detectable years later. Both benefits accrue to a different department and a later parliament than the one paying, which is a general reason good long-horizon policy is rare.

The quality condition is the part omitted from cost arguments. The measured benefits to children come from provision above a threshold of staff training, ratios and stability, and below that threshold the effects are neutral or negative. A cheap place is not a cheaper version of a good place; expanding capacity by relaxing the standards that produce the benefit purchases the appearance of a solution and discards the reason for wanting one.
